1:
What Nadab and Abihu did wrong is itemised most carefully by Ellicott, who counts four transgressions in one act. They each took his own censer rather than the sacred utensil of the sanctuary; they offered together, whereas the incense was to be offered by one; they encroached on the high priest's function, since by law he alone burnt incense in a censer while ordinary priests burnt it on the golden altar; and they chose an unauthorised time, apart from the morning and evening sacrifice. Henry presses a prior question, whether they had any business burning incense at all that day. The whole service of the inauguration was performed by Aaron himself, his sons only attending him, and Moses and Aaron alone entered the tabernacle; so the two were acting without orders or leave, being proud of the honour they had just been advanced to and ambitious of the most honourable part of the work at once. Having no authorised incense, since Moses had the custody of what was prepared, they used common incense from a strange fire. Wesley defines the term the same way, fire not taken from the altar as it ought to have been but from some common source, and adds the grammatical note that not commanding may here stand for forbidding.

Clarke supplies what none of the others do, a description of how incense was actually burnt, taken from the Jewish sources. One priest gathered the ashes from the altar into a golden vessel, a second brought a vessel of incense, a third brought a censer with fire and put coals on the altar, and the priest whose office it was strewed the incense on the fire at the governor's command, while all the people withdrew from between the porch and the altar. A hundred denaries' weight of incense was burnt daily, fifty in the morning and fifty in the evening, and when the priest had burnt it he bowed himself down and went out. Clarke then joins this to the scene in the gospel, where Zacharias burnt incense as his lot fell while the whole multitude prayed outside, and draws the lesson the arrangement was meant to teach: that the prayers of God's faithful people are pleasing to him, our High Priest adding incense to them by his mediation, since the priests under the law served to the example and shadow of heavenly things.

The severity is what needs defending, and Calvin defends it without pretending the offence looks grave. Apparently it was a light transgression to use strange fire, and their thoughtlessness would seem excusable, since they did not wantonly desire to pollute sacred things but, as often in matters of novelty, set about them too eagerly and were led into error by their precipitancy. The punishment will not please those arrogant people who do not hesitate superciliously to criticise God's judgments; but religion had to be sanctioned at its very commencement, for had God suffered Aaron's own sons to transgress with impunity they would afterwards have neglected the whole Law. Ellicott draws the lesson for the congregation watching: priests, though mediators between God and the people, are beset with the same infirmities as the laity and must not presume upon their office. He also catches the reversal in the fire itself, since the divine fire that had just come out to consume the sacrifices as a token of acceptance now comes out to consume the sacrificers, as the same gospel is to one a savour of life and to another of death. On what the fire did they agree: it slew without burning, since bodies and garments alike survived. Wesley compares the way the sword is said to devour and observes that lightning often kills without harming clothing; Gill calls the fire of the nature of lightning; Keil and Delitzsch infer the same from the men being carried out still in their priests' body-coats.
3:
The saying Moses quotes is nowhere on record, and they all notice it. Ellicott calls it another reference to a well-known divine communication through Moses not previously written down in the Pentateuch. Henry asks outright where God spoke this, and answers that we do not find the very words, though the substance was given when the priests who came near were told to sanctify themselves lest the Lord break forth upon them, and the whole tenour of the law said as much. Calvin says flatly that we shall seek in vain for what is referred to, reports that De Lyra assigns it to one Exodus passage and others to another, and quotes Willet's tart objection to a third answer: some think it was spoken but not written, as many things beside, and are of that mind because it gives them some show for their unwritten traditions. Willet's own solution, which Calvin passes on, is the charge at the consecration: keep ye the Lord's charge, that ye die not. Wesley takes the mildest line: Scripture contains only the heads of discourses, so the words were probably uttered by Moses in God's name though unrecorded, and the sense of them stands in many places. Gill notes only the purpose: to humble Aaron under the mighty hand of God.

On what the saying means, the division is between a duty and a purpose. Wesley lays both out: it may note their duty to sanctify God, demeaning themselves with the reverence that becomes his holiness, whence they gather the justice of the judgment; or God's purpose to sanctify himself by impartial punishment of all transgressors, however near to him they stand. Ellicott takes the second, making both verbs reflexive — I will sanctify myself in them that come near, I will glorify myself before all the people — explaining that God had sanctified Aaron's sons by the holy unction precisely that they might sanctify him by strict performance, and, having failed, he sanctified himself in them by the punishment. He adds that coming near to God is a standing designation for a priest. Calvin paraphrases the logic as a chain: when I have been sanctified by the priests themselves, whose dignity is highest, my glory will shine before the whole people. And he draws the conclusion that follows, that though God may punish whole bodies of obscure persons such lessons have little effect, while the punishment of men of illustrious condition draws almost all eyes to his judgments. Henry turns it on the reader: in worship we come nigh to God as spiritual priests.

The three words that close the verse draw the chapter's finest writing. Clarke renders them literally, and Aaron was dumb, asking how elegantly expressive this is of his parental affection, his sense of his sons' presumption and his submission to God's justice: the flower and hope of his family nipped in the bud and blasted, and he feeling it exquisitely as a father yet submitting without murmuring. Clarke then explains the silence: excessive grief stupefies the mind so that amazement and deep anguish prevent both tears and complaints — slight sorrows are loquacious, says Seneca, deep anguish has no voice. Ellicott hears the psalmist behind it, I was dumb, I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it; Wesley, that he neither murmured nor replied against God. Calvin gives the context that makes the restraint remarkable: a bitter stroke straight after their joy, two sons lost on the same day and at the same moment, with every temptation to murmur; the consolation Moses offers is that God had not dealt cruelly but had shown a just and profitable example, that their successors might be more attentive. Henry admires Moses rather than Aaron: whatever the rest were, he was composed, not displeased as David was in a like case, and kept decorum in the sanctuary — a brother born for adversity.
4:
Why Moses summoned these cousins only Ellicott presses, and his answer is the most interesting thing here. Uzziel was son of Kohath and younger brother of Amram, so uncle to Aaron, and his sons were Aaron's first cousins. Eleazar and Ithamar, as ordinary priests, might lawfully have carried out their own brothers, but were too much affected by so appalling a scene, and Moses wished to spare them. The harder question is why the two elder uncles are passed over, and Ellicott finds the reason in what happened afterwards: the discontent of their children with the election of Aaron's family, which later broke out in Korah's rebellion, had evidently begun to show itself, and men who suffered so signally for transgressing a divine institution had to be buried by men whose allegiance was unimpeachable. Calvin gives the simpler motive, that Eleazar and Ithamar were not to pollute themselves by carrying the bodies, and adds that all present may have been stupefied by terror. Wesley notes that Aaron and his sons were engaged in ministrations from which they were not called away for funerals; Gill and Clarke supply the genealogy without comment.

That they were carried out in their coats draws a real disagreement. Ellicott would render the word tunics, the long white garments in which they ministered, and explains what usually became of them: cast-off priestly dresses were converted into wick for the lamps, but these were buried with the men, since besides their uncleanness nobody would have used garments worn at so awful a visitation. Wesley offers two readings without choosing. Burial in the holy garments may have testified the respect still due the men notwithstanding their failure, God in judgment remembering mercy and sparing their souls when he took their lives; or the garments may have been polluted both by the sin and by the touch of the dead, so that God would not have them used again. On the place of burial they agree, outside the camp; Wesley gives sanitary and ceremonial reasons together, that the living might neither be annoyed by the scent of the dead nor defiled by their graves. Clarke turns this on a modern practice, calling burial within towns an impropriety and burial about and even within places dedicated to the worship of God an abomination at which piety and common sense alike shudder.

The ban on mourning is explained by its outward signs. Keil and Delitzsch insist the first phrase means not uncovering the head by removing a band or shaving it, but going about with the hair loose and dishevelled, its growth uncut. Ellicott describes the practice, mourners letting the hair fall wild over head and face, and notes that priests were forbidden even ordinarily to shave their heads or let their locks grow; he adds that Jews still tear their garments, let hair and nails grow and refrain from washing. Clarke gives two reasons: men serving in the sanctuary should avoid whatever incapacitates them, and the crime so plainly deserved what it received that mourning might be read as accusing divine justice of undue severity. Wesley states both and completes the command, the burning to be bewailed not so much in compassion for the dead as in sorrow for the tokens of divine displeasure. Ellicott explains why wrath would fall on all the people, given the connection between the nation and its representative. On the reason given, the anointing oil, Keil and Delitzsch supply the theology: it symbolises the Spirit of God, a Spirit of life having nothing in common with death but rather conquering it. Ellicott adds that the rule was kept strictly in the second Temple, an officiating priest hearing of a relative's death not quitting the sanctuary lest he seem to love the dead more than the living God. Gill reports Ben Gersom's inference that a priest who leaves his service is guilty of death.
8:
That God speaks to Aaron directly here, having hitherto sent everything through Moses, is explained three ways. Ellicott reads it as consolation and repair: half the priesthood struck down and the other half forbidden to mourn, the chief survivor might well conclude that God was displeased with the new pontificate altogether, and the people who had watched the punishment needed the office's prestige restored. Henry finds a more delicate reason. What was to be said might have been taken amiss from Moses, as though he suspected his brother of being a gluttonous man and a wine-bibber, so God says it himself — and Henry draws the general observation that we are so apt to resent cautions as accusations. Gill reports two Jewish explanations, Aben Ezra's that Aaron was addressed because he was a prophet, and Jarchi's that the communication was granted as a reward for his silence and to do him honour on that account, though Gill himself thinks the plain reason is that Aaron was now high priest and in the execution of his office.

Whether the prohibition implies that Nadab and Abihu were drunk is the chapter's liveliest question, and they are genuinely split. Gill thinks the placing of the law gives the suspicion some reason, and reconstructs the occasion: they had feasted that day on the peace offerings and drunk freely, it being their first day in office, so it may be supposed they were elated and merry and drank more than they should. Clarke traces the opinion to the cabalistical commentator Baal Hatturim and others, who supposed the two attempted the divine service in a state of inebriation. Ellicott dates it earlier, the view being current at least as early as the time of Christ, and reports that the Palestinian Chaldee inserts the gloss outright: as thy sons did who died by the burning fire. Wesley calls it not improbable but rests nothing on it, since drunkenness is odious enough in itself, especially in a minister and most of all during his administration of sacred things, for God to forbid all occasions of it. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the law's occasion lies in the event just recorded while refusing the inference some commentators draw from it. Two counter-arguments stand on record: Scripture nowhere states it, and the offenders had been ministering since early morning.

On the second term Clarke does the lexicography, deriving it from a root meaning to inebriate and making it cover any fermented liquor; he notes the same pair of words used of John the Baptist, cites Jerome that any intoxicating drink is called sicera whether of corn, apples, honey or dates, and suggests our word cider probably descends from it. Calvin accepts Jerome's account but would make it exacter, restricting the term to liquors expressed from fruits, in whose sweetness there is nearly as much to tempt men as in wine; and he sets the priests under the Nazarites' rule, both allowed the richest foods but confined to water, since abstinence in drink conduces to frugality — few being intemperate in eating who do not also love wine. Keil and Delitzsch make it a drink of barley with dates or honey, and enter the distinction the next verse requires: common is a wider notion than unclean, everything counting as common that is not fitted for the sanctuary, even what is allowable in daily use. Henry limits the ban to the time of ministration, since it was never expected that every priest be a Nazarite, and observes that drunkenness is bad in any man but especially scandalous in ministers, who of all men ought to have the clearest heads and cleanest hearts. Ellicott closes on the teaching office, quoting Ezekiel's charge against priests who put no difference between holy and profane; Wesley adds that the devil, being God's ape, required the same abstinence of his own priests.
12:
Why the ordinary instructions are repeated now is answered the same way by all. Henry draws the principle from the resumption itself, that afflictions should quicken us to our duty rather than take us off from it, and finds meaning in the phrase about the sons that were left: Aaron is to take comfort that God spared him two, and the two spared are engaged by that sparing to proceed rather than fly off. Four priests had been consecrated together, two were taken and two left, so those remaining should endeavour to fill the places of the gone by double care and diligence. Calvin gives the psychological reason: they were as yet little practised in the rites, and what had happened must have made them anxious, their consternation so confounding their senses that they could not apply themselves with composure and the offering would have been improperly made. Wesley adds a second motive: if grief had made them neglect the meat God prescribed, the abstinence would have been at once a signification of the sorrow they had been forbidden and a fresh transgression. Ellicott states the anxiety plainly: having lost two sons for violating the sacrificial rules, Aaron and the survivors must be guarded against transgressing any other part of them.

The instruction itself turns on a distinction Henry states as a second lesson in discrimination. The priests must learn not only to put a difference between the holy and the unholy, as they had just been told, but also, among the things they were to eat, between what was most holy and what was only holy. The remainder of the meat offering fell in the first class, and Ellicott sets out what that entailed: apart from the handful burnt on the altar the whole belonged to the priests, it was to be eaten beside the altar within the court of the tent of meeting, and being most holy it could be eaten only by the male members of the priestly families. Gill guards the phrase about the holy place against a natural misreading: it means not the holy place properly so called but the court of the tabernacle, the point being that the food was not to be carried out and eaten in their own tents as other portions might. Ellicott would render it a holy place rather than the holy place, meaning any part of the sacred court; Wesley locates it more exactly still, in the court near the altar of burnt offerings. Calvin notices what the reason given does, since Moses sets before them the authority of God, to which the priesthood ought to be subject as founded upon it.

The wave breast and heave shoulder belong to the lower grade, and the difference shows in three ways. Ellicott notes first that they come from the peace offering the nation had brought, and that being assigned to the priests for the maintenance of their families they might be eaten anywhere within the camp, provided the place was not defiled by ceremonial uncleanness. Gill gives the practical test, that the place must be clean and free of polluted persons such as lepers, and reports Jarchi's rule that these lighter holy things might be eaten in every city, the camp being where lepers did not come. Wesley draws out the consequence that matters most, that they could be eaten in any place where the women might come as well as the men, since the daughters of a priest might eat these as well as his sons, whether they were maids or widows or divorced. On the closing verse Gill and Ellicott agree about the subject of the verb: it is not the priests who bring the breast and shoulder but the offerers, who devote these portions and hand them to the officiating priest. Clarke passes the whole passage over with a cross-reference to his fuller treatment earlier.
16:
Which goat Moses sought is answered differently by the Jewish sources, and Gill sets them out. The Targum of Jonathan counts three goats that day — the new moon, the people's sin offering, and the one Nahshon offered at the dedication — and has Aaron's house burn all three; Jarchi counts three but says only the new-moon goat was burnt; Ben Gersom explains the diligence of the search: that one was always to be offered, no temporary affair. Gill prefers the people's sin offering, since it is not certain the others were offered that day while this one was. Clarke identifies it the same way, the goat offered that day for the sins of priests and people, and states plainly what happened: through the confusion following the death of Nadab and Abihu it was burnt instead of eaten. Ellicott supplies the motive: Eleazar and Ithamar, overwhelmed with grief, could not eat, and since none but priests might partake they burnt the flesh to prevent its corruption — the more readily because the flesh of Aaron's own sin offering had just been burnt outside the camp.

That the anger falls on the sons and not the father two of them notice, giving the same reason. Ellicott points out that eating the flesh was quite as much Aaron's duty, and supposes Moses omitted his name to spare the pontiff's honour in the people's sight. Wesley says the same and adds that Aaron was overwhelmed with sorrow, and rebuking him before his sons might have exposed him to contempt Wesley says the same and adds that Aaron was overwhelmed with sorrow, and that rebuking him before his sons might have exposed him to contempt — though a reproof directed at them would reach him too.mdash; though a reproof aimed at them would reach him too. Wesley catches the edge in the phrase about the sons left alive: being left, they ought of all men to have taken warning. Calvin is harsher, turning the incident into a lesson about teaching. Moses had told them what to do with the goat, and the sacrifice he performed himself was a visible instruction, enough even for children; yet they perverted it as if they had neither heard nor seen anything. From this he infers that however exquisite the ability of teachers, their work is fruitless without obedient scholars of retentive memory; and that when God inculcates a thing repeatedly his labour is not superfluous, since we do not understand what we seem to.

Ellicott states the rule with its exception: a sin offering whose blood was not carried into the sanctuary had to be eaten by the priests as part of the expiatory rite, while one whose blood was carried in had to be burnt — and the blood of the people's offering here was not carried in. Gill puts the charge precisely: the fault was not eating it in the wrong place, but not eating it. Wesley explains why the blood stayed outside: Aaron was not yet admitted into the holy place till he had prepared the way by the sacrifices in the court. The phrase about bearing the congregation's iniquity carries the one real dispute. Ellicott prefers to remove rather than to bear, the expression often meaning to bear away or forgive, and the Septuagint, Chaldee and Syriac render it so; but the received English follows the Vulgate, and with it the Reformers and several modern expositors, supported by the sense the phrase carries elsewhere. On that reading the priest, by eating and so incorporating the victim on which the offerer had laid his guilt, actually took the sin away, neutralising it by the sanctifying power of his office. Wesley states the milder version: the portion rewards their service, by which they take away the people's sins in offering the sacrifices through which God is reconciled to penitent offerers. Clarke refers the reader back.
19:
Aaron answers a charge laid against his sons, and Gill explains why. What Moses said was said in his presence though not addressed to him, and Aaron was sensible that he was pointed at and that whatever blame there was lay as much on him; so he takes the reply on himself and excuses the act as well as he can. Ellicott traces the shape of the excuse and finds it carefully built. Aaron begins by observing that all the other sacrificial duties performed that day, before the calamity, were done in strict accordance with the prescribed ritual, which shows they never meant to transgress deliberately. Only then does he come to what happened, that while they performed those rites his other two sons transgressed and were struck down, overwhelming the survivors and rendering them unfit to partake. Only then does he submit the conclusion, that unfitted as they were by mourning and by the sense of their own sinfulness, their eating so solemn a meal would not have been acceptable. Wesley states the defence in miniature: they had done the substance of the thing though mistaking one circumstance, and the portion was not to be eaten with sorrow but with rejoicing and thanksgiving.

Clarke gives the speech in his own words and calls it appropriate and dignified. God certainly commanded me to eat of the sin offering, he has Aaron say, but when such things have happened to me, could it be good in the sight of the Lord? Does he not expect that I should feel as a father under such afflicting circumstances? Clarke then turns from the case to the principle, in the warmest passage of the chapter: to human nature God has given the privilege of weeping in affliction, and in his infinite kindness has ordained that tears, the mere external evidences of our grief, should be the outlets of our sorrows and tend to exhaust the cause from which they flow. Ellicott explains why the charge was addressed to the sons when the father was equally liable: the lawgiver abstained from anger against the pontiff because of his office's supreme dignity, which he would not lower in the people's sight — a restraint Aaron was fully sensible of.

That Moses was content Ellicott reads as the most human moment in the book. He acknowledged Aaron's plea to be just and that he had himself spoken hastily — a remarkable instance, Ellicott says, of his humility and of the human side of his nature; and Jewish tradition has from time immemorial ascribed the mistake to Moses rather than Aaron. The Palestinian Chaldee makes the concession explicit, having Moses approve the explanation and send a herald through the camp to say that it was he from whom the law had been hidden, and his brother Aaron who brought it to his remembrance. Gill is more forensic: the case had a real difficulty, since the flesh of a sin offering was in some circumstances to be eaten and not burnt and in others burnt and not eaten, and this being the first such offering the mistake was easily made — which may be why Moses sought the goat so diligently. Clarke grants the argument had good sense and strong reason, that Moses as a reasonable man felt its force, and that since God showed no displeasure at an irregularity so far justified by necessity he urged it no further. He will not let the chapter end there, insisting that God has given full proof that he will not suffer human institutions to take the place of his own prescribed worship, and that those who put their own creeds in place of divine ordinances must expect to give an awful account. Wesley closes more kindly: Aaron sincerely aimed at pleasing God, and those who do so find he is not extreme to mark what is done amiss.
